answer.summary: Choose design partners for startup-friendliness and a person aligned with the founder’s vision who welcomes candid feedback and an unfinished product. Set honest expectations, use the relationship to learn and guide product direction, and don’t assume it will turn into a large rollout.

sections.heading: Choose for alignment and willingness to participate
sections.content: Look for a company with a startup-friendly reputation, and assess the individual: are they excited to give feedback, buy into where the company is going, see the opportunity similarly to the founder, and accept that the early tool will be rough? Abel emphasizes choosing someone aligned with what they are getting into, not just an attractive logo.

sections.heading: Be candid about the product and the commitment
sections.content: Explain what the product can and cannot do today, what you expect to allow them to do over the next six months, and that it may be “really ugly” with little built yet. Invite them to join the journey and contribute their voice. Abel warns that overselling the design-partner phase or promising a full rollout can cause frustration, churn, or cancellation; honesty builds trust.

sections.heading: Use the partnership to learn and guide product direction
sections.content: Treat design partners as guides for understanding the problem, rather than assuming they will become a million-dollar pipeline: they can be the hardest logos to upsell from design partner to full rollout. Ask them to co-author the scope of work; Abel says this can help turn a customer into a guide and reveal whether they already have a process or strategy for solving the problem. If they do not, she says they cannot yet buy the technology, so selling a service can let the founder educate them, gain the logo, and show revenue, though it is not recurring revenue. Listen closely to their feedback, but retain founder clarity about the destination: Abel describes much of it as potentially off-direction, while the valuable minority can reveal something important the founder had not considered. The percentages she cites—80% and 20%—are her example of that pattern, not a guarantee.

sections.heading: A practical sequence (synthesis)
sections.content: Taken together, Abel’s recommendations suggest: identify a startup-friendly organization and aligned contact; disclose the product’s current limits and near-term expectations; invite the contact to help shape the scope; use the work and feedback to learn while the founder keeps responsibility for product direction; and treat rollout as a possibility, not an assumed outcome.
